summary_text:
On January 8, 2024, the patient's left arm was pulled into industrial machinery, crushing and nearly severing it above the elbow. Factory responders applied a tourniquet and dismantled the machine to free him before EMS arrived; on scene he presented with a cold, pulseless hand, exposed bone, and a GCS of 11 with a reported brief loss of consciousness. He was transferred to Midwest Regional's trauma unit, where Dr. David Cho documented complete traumatic amputation at the level between the shoulder and elbow, with the brachial artery and major nerves completely transected and massive soft tissue loss. X-ray and CT angiography confirmed a comminuted, displaced supracondylar humerus fracture with open segmental forearm and hand fractures and carpal disintegration, and angiography confirmed the vascular disruption. The limb was deemed unsalvageable. He received two units of packed red blood cells for traumatic shock and was taken emergently to the OR.

That same day, Dr. Marcus Vance performed a left transhumeral amputation, sectioning the humerus at the junction of the middle and distal thirds, ligating and dividing the brachial artery, and performing traction neurectomy of the median, ulnar, and radial nerves with bupivacaine 0.5% injection before myofascial closure. He recovered in the ICU, was started on a Dilaudid PCA, Ancef, and gabapentin, and was later transitioned to oral oxycodone and gabapentin 300mg three times daily. A JP drain was removed January 12, and he was discharged on a course of Cefdinir and gabapentin.

By his February 12, 2024 follow-up, the stump had healed well, but he reported phantom limb pain rated 7/10 and severe hypersensitivity at the distal stump, prompting an increase in gabapentin to 600mg three times daily, a desensitization therapy referral, and a shrinker sock fitting. The pain did not resolve. At five months out, on June 18, 2024, Dr. Cho identified a tender, mobile 1.5 cm nodule at the medial residual border reproducing electric shock sensations into the phantom hand — a traumatic neuroma of the ulnar/median nerve stumps — after conservative management failed. On November 12, 2024, he excised the neuroma (measuring 1.8 x 1.4 cm) and transposed the median and ulnar nerve stumps into the triceps muscle, securing them with 5-0 epineural sutures.

Prosthetic rehabilitation followed: a myoelectric transhumeral prosthesis was fitted and calibrated on February 5, 2025, with electrode training, grasping drills, and progressive wear-time and bilateral coordination work through the spring. Despite intermittent no-shows in May and November 2025, he completed a final functional capacity evaluation on June 15, 2026, and was discharged June 22, 2026, with near-normal left shoulder range of motion, cleared to return to modified light/medium duty at his employer.

Dr. Vance's transhumeral amputation procedure details are accurately described.

Phantom pain, hypersensitivity, gabapentin increase, and referrals are covered, though pain score is misstated as 7/10 instead of 8/10.
Neuroma finding and symptoms are described, but misattributed to Dr. Cho instead of Dr. Vance.
Excision size, transposition, and suture details are accurately described and correctly attributed to Dr. Vance.
No mention of Liberty Mutual hold or authorization delay pending peer review.
No specific ROM measurements, sleep issues, or work status at rehab intake are mentioned.
Fitting/calibration date mentioned but no component details (socket, elbow, hand) or 80% signal accuracy figure.
